exercises.prompt:
What does this print? Write it exactly as R prints it, with single spaces between the numbers.

```r
x <- c(5, 10, 15, 20, 25, 30)
x + c(1, 100)
```

feedback.message: Not yet. The shorter vector (1, 100) is recycled: 1, 100, 1, 100, 1, 100.

hints: The vector c(1, 100) is repeated until it has six elements.
exercises.solution: `c(1, 100)` is recycled to 1, 100, 1, 100, 1, 100 and added element by element: 6, 110, 16, 120, 26, 130. Six is a multiple of two, so there is no warning. (R pads numbers to equal width when printing, so its output shows extra spaces: `[1]   6 110  16 120  26 130`.)

exercises.prompt:
What number does this print?

```r
x <- c(4, 8, 15, 16, 23, 42)
x[-c(1, 2)][2]
```

feedback.message: Not yet. `x[-c(1, 2)]` removes the first two elements first; then [2] picks from what is left.
Not yet. After removing 4 and 8, the remaining vector is 15, 16, 23, 42. Its second element is …

hints: Work from left to right: first drop positions 1 and 2, then take position 2 of the result.
exercises.solution: `x[-c(1, 2)]` drops 4 and 8, leaving 15, 16, 23, 42. Indexing that with `[2]` gives its second element, **16**.

feedback.message: That is sort(): the values in order. order() returns positions.
Not yet. That is the rank of each element (rank()). order() lists which position comes first, second, …

hints: The smallest value, 2, is at position 3. Which position holds the next smallest?
exercises.solution: `order()` returns the positions that would sort the vector: the smallest value (2) is at position 3, then 3 at position 1, then 7 at position 4, then 9 at position 2. So `[1] 3 1 4 2`. Using these positions, `x[order(x)]` gives the sorted values 2 3 7 9.

exercises.prompt:
Which names does this print? List them.

```r
ages <- c(Lea = 34, Ravi = 17, Su = 25, Tom = 15, Uma = 41)
names(ages)[ages >= 18 & ages < 40]
```

feedback.message: Not yet. Uma is 41, so `ages < 40` is FALSE for her.

hints: Build the logical vector first: for each person, is the age at least 18 and below 40?
The logical vector lines up with names(ages), so it can index it.
exercises.solution: `ages >= 18 & ages < 40` is TRUE for Lea (34) and Su (25) only. Using it to index `names(ages)` returns `"Lea" "Su"`.

exercises.prompt:
This script prints two numbers. What is the **second**?

```r
x <- c(2, NA, 6, 8)
sum(x > 3, na.rm = TRUE)
length(x[x > 3])
```

feedback.message: Not yet. That is the first number. In `x[x > 3]`, the NA in the logical index produces an NA element in the result.

hints: Indexing with NA does not drop the element; it gives NA.
exercises.solution: `x > 3` is `FALSE NA TRUE TRUE`. The sum with `na.rm = TRUE` counts 2. But `x[x > 3]` is `NA 6 8`: a logical index that is NA yields an NA element. Its length is **3**. To filter safely, use `x[which(x > 3)]` or `x[!is.na(x) & x > 3]`.

exercises.prompt: You want to keep the elements of `temps` that are below 0 or above 35. Which expression does that?

options.label: `temps[temps < 0 | temps > 35]`
options.feedback: Yes. `|` combines the two logical vectors element by element, and the result indexes temps.

options.label: `temps[temps < 0 || temps > 35]`
options.feedback: Not yet. `||` works on single values only; with vectors it is an error in R 4.3 and later.

options.label: `temps[temps < 0 & temps > 35]`
options.feedback: Not yet. No temperature is both below 0 and above 35, so this keeps nothing.

options.label: `if (temps < 0 | temps > 35) temps`
options.feedback: Not yet. `if` needs a single TRUE or FALSE; it cannot filter a vector.

hints: For vectors, use the single-character operators.
exercises.solution: `temps[temps < 0 | temps > 35]`. The single `|` and `&` are vectorised and are what you use inside an index. The doubled `||` and `&&` are for single conditions in `if`.

exercises.prompt: A function loops with `for (i in 1:length(x))`. What happens when it is given an empty vector?

options.label: The loop runs twice, with i = 1 and then i = 0.
options.feedback: Yes. `1:0` is the sequence 1, 0. Use seq_along(x), which is empty for an empty x.

options.label: The loop body never runs.
options.feedback: Not yet. That is what you want, and what seq_along(x) gives, but 1:0 is not empty.

options.label: R raises an error before the loop starts.
options.feedback: Not yet. 1:0 is perfectly valid; it just counts down.

options.label: The loop runs once, with i = 1.
options.feedback: Not yet. The colon operator counts down from 1 to 0, giving two values.

hints: What is length(c())? What does 1:0 produce?
exercises.solution: `length(x)` is 0, so the loop iterates over `1:0`, which is `1 0`: two iterations with meaningless indices. `seq_along(x)` (or `seq_len(length(x))`) returns an empty sequence, so the loop correctly does nothing.
